notes.h: Methods of aerobic and anaerobic training
notes.b: Different sports tax the body's energy systems in different ways, so there is no single best way to train. These three methods mainly target the aerobic system (which uses oxygen to release energy for long efforts) and the anaerobic system (which works without oxygen for short, intense efforts).
points: Continuous training is steady, moderate-intensity exercise without rest for at least 20 minutes in the aerobic zone (about 60 to 80% of maximum heart rate). It works the aerobic system, so it develops cardio-respiratory endurance (heart and lungs) and muscular endurance.
Continuous training suits activities that are themselves continuous, such as distance running, swimming and cycling, because the training matches what the event demands.

Interval training alternates periods of work with periods of rest or recovery. Its demand is set by three things: the work-to-rest ratio (how long you work compared with how long you recover), the number of repetitions and the number of sets.

Short, high-intensity intervals with longer recovery develop speed and anaerobic capacity, because the rest lets you repeat hard efforts. Longer intervals at lower intensity develop aerobic fitness instead.
Interval training suits intermittent sports (bursts of effort with pauses) such as hurling, soccer and basketball, because it copies the pattern of work and rest in the game.

Fartlek (Swedish for speed play) is continuous running with changes of pace and terrain, for example jogging, sprinting between lamp posts and running uphill. It trains the aerobic and anaerobic systems together, so it suits games players.
notes.tip: If asked to name a method of training for speed, give interval training (short, high-intensity work) and name an activity it suits, such as soccer. Always link the method to the energy system and the activity.

notes.h: Methods of strength, power and flexibility training
notes.b: Muscles can be trained to work for longer, to produce more force, to produce force quickly, or to move through a bigger range. Each of these aims has its own method.
points: Circuit training is a series of stations worked in turn with set work and rest times. It can be designed for muscular endurance, strength, cardio-respiratory endurance or sport skills, depending on the exercises chosen at the stations.
Resistance (weight) training means working against a load such as free weights, machines or body weight, with exercises such as squats, lunges, presses, rows and curls.

In resistance training, the number of repetitions decides the result: heavy loads with few repetitions build strength, while light loads with many repetitions build muscular endurance (the ability to keep a muscle working).

Plyometric training uses jumping, bounding and hopping. A lengthening contraction on landing is followed immediately by a forceful shortening contraction on take-off, which develops power for jumping and sprinting.
Plyometrics puts heavy stress on muscles and joints, so it needs a strength base, a forgiving surface and low volume. This means it is not for beginners.
Static stretching holds a stretch still at mild tension. It is best in the cool-down, when the body is warm and the aim is to relax muscles and keep or improve range.
Dynamic stretching is controlled movement through the full range of a joint, such as leg swings, and it is used in the warm-up to prepare the muscles for the movements to come.

PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) stretching has four steps: stretch the muscle, contract it against resistance from a partner, relax, then stretch further. It gives the greatest gains in range.
notes.tip: Examiners ask how weight training and circuit training could improve a chosen component, so say which load or station design you would use. Never recommend plyometrics for beginners without the strength-base caution. For flexibility, name a method with an example activity.

notes.b: The skill in comparing methods is matching each one to what the activity actually demands. The same method can be ideal for one sport and poor for another.
points: Hurling is stop-start, so interval training and fartlek suit it better than continuous training. Resistance and plyometric work add power for striking and jumping.
Distance swimming depends on the aerobic system, so continuous and long-interval training develop the fitness the event needs.
Gymnastics relies on flexibility and body-weight strength rather than long efforts, so flexibility training and body-weight strength work matter more than long aerobic sessions.
The best method depends on the energy systems and fitness components the activity demands.
notes.tip: When asked to explain methods for a named activity, give the method, the energy system or component it develops, and why the activity needs it.

notes.h: Training in the activity and outside the activity
notes.b: Training can take place in the sport itself or in other forms of exercise that build the same fitness. Each approach has strengths, and good programmes use both.
points: Training in the activity uses conditioned games and sport-specific drills. It is specific (it copies the real movements), motivating, and trains skill under fatigue, which is when skill usually breaks down in matches.

Training outside the activity includes gym-based resistance training, plyometrics, swimming or cycling as cross-training (training in a different sport), and yoga or Pilates for flexibility and core strength.
Training outside the activity can overload specific components precisely, build a fitness base, add variety, and reduce overuse of the sport's repeated movements.
The limitation is that training outside the activity is less specific, so it must be linked back to the activity's movements and demands.
For a hurler, resistance training builds the strength and power for long striking and winning dropping balls, while yoga improves hip and shoulder range for the swing.
notes.tip: If asked to identify two approaches to training outside a named activity, pick two (for example resistance training and yoga or Pilates) and say how each helps the activity.

notes.h: Designing a fitness programme from test data
notes.b: A good programme starts from evidence, not guesswork. Fitness test results show what to train, and the rest of the design follows in five steps.
points: 1. Use the fitness test results to identify the weakest components that matter most for the activity, so effort goes where it will help performance most.
2. Set goals for those components.
3. Select training methods suited to each goal.
4. Apply FITT (frequency, intensity, time, type) and the principles of training. Plan sessions per week across several weeks with progression, a warm-up and cool-down in each session, and rest days.
5. Re-test at the end to evaluate the programme and adjust it, because the new results show whether the goals were met.

Illustrative six-week plan (example values only) for a soccer player whose tests show weak speed and agility: two speed and agility sessions a week (sprints and cone drills with full recovery), one resistance session for leg strength, and one fartlek run.
In the same illustrative plan, repetitions rise every two weeks, week four is lighter, and the player is re-tested in week six.
notes.tip: For a programme question, link each training method to a weakness shown in the test results, then show progression, rest and a re-test. Label any figures you invent as examples.

notes.b: Training is the stimulus, but the body improves while it recovers afterwards. Recovery strategies help this process along and keep performers ready for the next session.
points: Adaptation happens during recovery, not during the session. If recovery is adequate, the body rebuilds slightly above its previous level, which is called supercompensation.
Cool-down means light activity and stretching, which help remove waste products and return the body to rest.

Rehydration replaces fluid and electrolytes (salts) lost in sweat. Refuelling soon after exercise matters too: carbohydrate restores muscle glycogen (the muscles' stored fuel) and protein repairs muscle tissue.
Sleep supports recovery because most tissue repair and growth takes place during sleep.
Active recovery is a light session, such as an easy swim the day after a match, which keeps blood flowing to the muscles.

Massage and foam rolling reduce muscle tightness and soreness. Cold-water immersion reduces inflammation and soreness after intense exercise, and compression garments may reduce swelling and soreness.
Planned rest days and lighter weeks prevent overtraining, which is when training outpaces recovery. There is more on its signs in Safe practice.
notes.tip: Explain two recovery strategies by giving each one with its reason, for example carbohydrate restores muscle glycogen, or sleep supports tissue repair. A bare list of strategies earns little.

notes.b: Training hard all year would lead to exhaustion, not peak form. Periodisation avoids this by planning the year in stages, so the performer is at their best when it matters.
points: Periodisation divides a training plan into planned phases or cycles, each with a specific aim, so that volume, intensity and recovery vary systematically to bring the performer to peak performance at target competitions.

Cycles run from longest to shortest. The macrocycle is the long-term plan, often a year or a season. The mesocycle is a block of several weeks, often 4 to 6, with one focus, such as building strength. The microcycle is usually one week of sessions.
The preparation phase builds general fitness first, then specific fitness and skills.
In the competition phase, fitness is maintained and the performer peaks for key events. Tapering before the main event reduces training volume while keeping intensity, so the performer arrives fresh.
The transition phase is active rest and recovery after the season.
Coaches use periodisation so the performer peaks at the right time, develops qualities in a logical order, avoids overtraining and injury, and stays motivated through variety.
Peaking for a single major event, such as an Olympic Games every four years, uses a long-term plan built from these cycles, with each year's macrocycle building towards the target.
notes.tip: When matching timeframes, keep the order macro > meso > micro: a full year is the macrocycle, a block of weeks the mesocycle, one week the microcycle. Define periodisation, then give reasons coaches use it.

factCards.definition: Macrocycle: a year or season. Mesocycle: several weeks, often 4 to 6. Microcycle: usually a week.

factCards.term: Three phases of a periodised year
factCards.definition: Preparation (general then specific), competition (maintain and peak, with a taper), transition (active rest).

factCards.term: Two approaches to training outside the activity
factCards.definition: Resistance training in the gym; yoga or Pilates (also cross-training such as swimming or cycling).

factCards.term: Two recovery strategies and why they work
factCards.definition: Carbohydrate and protein soon after exercise restore glycogen and repair muscle; sleep allows tissue repair and growth.

questions.prompt: Explain periodisation and outline its importance in preparing for a major championship.
questions.model: Periodisation is dividing a training plan into planned phases or cycles, each with its own aim, so that volume, intensity and recovery vary systematically to bring the athlete to peak performance at a target competition. The macrocycle covers the year or season and is divided into mesocycles of several weeks with one focus, which are made up of weekly microcycles. The year moves through a preparation phase (general base, then specific fitness), a competition phase (maintenance and peaking) and a transition phase (active rest). It is important because an athlete cannot hold peak form all year: it lets the coach build qualities in a logical order, plan recovery to avoid overtraining and injury, and taper before the championship so the athlete arrives fit and fresh. For a championship held every four years, each year's plan builds towards that target.

questions.prompt: Explain two recovery strategies athletes use after exercise to support adaptation.
questions.model: 1. Refuelling with carbohydrate and protein soon after exercise: hard training depletes muscle glycogen and damages muscle fibres. Carbohydrate restores glycogen so the next session can be performed at the right intensity, and protein supplies the amino acids needed to repair and rebuild muscle, which is how strength and endurance gains are made. 2. Sleep: most tissue repair and growth happens during sleep, so adequate sleep allows the body to adapt to the training load; poor sleep slows recovery and raises the risk of overtraining and injury.

questions.prompt: Name and describe two methods of fitness training suitable for a games player.
questions.model: 1. Interval training: periods of hard work alternated with recovery, such as six 30-second runs at near-maximum effort with 90 seconds of walking. This copies the stop-start pattern of a game and develops speed and the ability to recover between efforts. 2. Fartlek training: continuous running with changes of pace and terrain, such as jogging and then sprinting between markers. It trains the aerobic and anaerobic systems together, as a match does.
